subject: 8D2A3C574FE5EDD77156FE2FD3CEE657
introduction: When ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wanted to encourage persecuted or obscure Bahá’ís he told them about the first Christians: fishermen whom nobody thought worth noticing, mocked and beaten in their lifetime, opposed by the learned of their own religion and then by Rome, and in the end honoured by the world that had despised them. This guide gathers those passages. The New Testament supplies most of the scenes: “the offscouring of all things”, the apostles “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer”, Stephen, the roll of Hebrews 11. Tacitus and Tertullian give the Roman side from outside and inside the Church. Two cautions belong with the readings. The Pharisee who counselled restraint, Gamaliel, is in Acts as well; and the Gospel language about “the Jews” as persecutors, which the readings repeat, has a long and terrible afterlife that a study group should not pass over.
questions: Why do new religions so often begin among people of no standing, and meet their first opposition from the learned of the old?
What made persecution fail, according to readings 19 to 22?
Gamaliel was a Pharisee. What does his speech do to the picture of “the Pharisees” in these readings?
The readings speak of “the Jews” and “the Israelites” as persecutors. How should that language be read and spoken today?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses this history to console. What exactly is the consolation?

outside.why: The disciples scoffed at and vilified. Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things.
At the beginning of a Cause, common souls of no importance advance. God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
“What station or worth do fishermen have?” They perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, and they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Always under taunt and persecution in their lifetime. If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
Beaten by the multitude. They departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name.
Calumny and cruelty brought on the apostles for the sake of faith. They stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.

“By the Israelites”: the readings follow the Gospels and Acts in naming the persecutors as Jews, language later used to justify the persecution of Jews by Christians. Paul, himself persecuted by his own people, refused the inference: hath God cast away his people? God forbid; for I also am an Israelite. How should a reader hold these readings’ language in the light of that history?
Men like Caiaphas, who came in their own name, were accepted. I am come in my Father’s name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive.
A thousand Pharisees worshipping were not accepted. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are.
They followed the superstitions of the Pharisees. Ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law.
The first condition: that Christ would come from an unknown place. We know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is.
Denied by those who knew the Law in its minutiae, accepted by fishermen. Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
The early centuries of reproach. They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: of whom the world was not worthy.
They accepted every trial. Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

The standard of the Roman emperors was shattered for their opposition. A Roman’s account of Nero’s victims: mockery of every sort was added to their deaths; covered with the skins of beasts, they were torn by dogs.
Emperors and kings persecuted, to no effect. Tertullian: if the Tiber rises, if the Nile does not, if there is famine or pestilence, the cry is at once, the Christians to the lion!

A king saw that killing Christians bore no fruit and took counsel. Gamaliel, a Pharisee, to the council: refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
Converts were not attracted by hospitals. See, they say, how they love one another.
The pious left without a portion; Peter, John and Andrew received. The publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.

shortfall: Readings 4, 10, 14, 15, 18, 21, 23 and 26 repeat the contrast of fishermen and Pharisees or tell stories for which no source could be set.
